steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
General-Purpose computing on Graphics Processing Units (GPGPU) is used to get better solutions in many fields, for example computer vision, graph processing, biomedical, financial analysis, and physical simulation. This is because of the computational power of Graphics Processing Units (GPU). So these devices are used in High-Performance Computing (HPC) to solve real-world problems. But current GPU devices also have drawbacks and limitations that have to be considered when a new algorithm is designed, such as the architecture, memory bandwidth, amount of memory, and memory speed. Even with these limitations, it is possible to implement a solver that reaches impressive results and new solutions.

In this paper, we propose a parallel self-avoiding walk algorithm for the Low-Autocorrelation Binary Sequences (LABS) problem, which is a formidable computational challenge. In this problem we have to find binary sequences S_{L}^{*} of length L that have the highest value of the merit factor F, as shown in Eq. (1). These sequences are important in many areas, like communication engineering, statistical mechanics, chemistry, cryptography, and mathematics.

In our previous works we proposed two solvers, lssOrel and xLastovka. Both of them are stochastic solvers that use the mechanism for fast evaluation of neighbor solutions, and both are limited to skew-symmetric sequences. The main difference between them is the memory usage that guides the search process. lssOrel uses a self-avoiding walk and a small hash table so that the same pivot is not visited twice. xLastovka on the other hand stores a large number of promising sequences in a priority queue and uses them to manage the search process. Both solvers only explore the skew-symmetric search space. This means that the dimension of the search space is reduced by almost half (D=\frac{L+1}{2}), and so the solver can find (sub)-optimal sequences a lot faster. The skew-symmetric search space is only defined for odd instances, as shown in Eq. (2), and the optimal skew-symmetric sequences may not be optimal for the entire search space.

Other authors proposed a hybrid architecture that uses both CPU and GPGPU processing units for an agent-based memetic computational system. They used this system to solve the LABS problem on the entire search space with steepest descent and tabu search. The maximum speedup they got was 46 with tabu search for L=128. This result shows that GPGPU processing units are useful for solving the LABS problem. Because of this work, we proposed the sokol skew solver for skew-symmetric sequences. It is implemented for NVIDIA GPU devices using the CUDA (Compute Unified Device Architecture) toolkit. The sokol skew solver uses parallel self-avoiding walks and a recently published mechanism for efficient neighborhood evaluation. Both of them are computationally efficient and they also need only a small amount of memory. Together they are a suitable algorithm that prevents cycling and a mechanism that can use GPU devices to speed up the energy calculation. With them, sokol skew got a speedup of 387 compared to the sequential CPU solver, and so it found new best-known sequences.

- Predictive model, results, trend
  - stopping-condition model from instances L=71 to L=119
  - stopping conditions for optimal skew-symmetric sequences with probability 99%
  - found all known + seven new best-known sequences, all odd L=121 to L=223
  - larger instances up to L=247: all known + several new best-known
  - probability achieved sequences are optimal, from the model
  - trend model of best merit factors: increase slightly with length, flatter for larger sizes
- Contributions
  1. parallel search with self-avoiding walks, skew-symmetric, uses GPGPU
  2. skew-symmetric sequences optimal with probability 99% (model), L=121 to L=223
  3. seventeen new best-known sequences for L\leq 247
  4. trend of merit factors from new best-known sequences
- Outline: Sec 2 related work; Sec 3 sokol skew; Sec 4 experiments, analysis, results; Sec 5 conclusion

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
General-Purpose computing on Graphics Processing Units (GPGPU) is used to get better solutions in many fields, for example computer vision, graph processing, biomedical, financial analysis, and physical simulation. This is because of the computational power of Graphics Processing Units (GPU). So these devices are used in High-Performance Computing (HPC) to solve real-world problems. But current GPU devices also have drawbacks and limitations that have to be considered when a new algorithm is designed, such as the architecture, memory bandwidth, amount of memory, and memory speed. Even with these limitations, it is possible to implement a solver that reaches impressive results and new solutions.

In this paper, we propose a parallel self-avoiding walk algorithm for the Low-Autocorrelation Binary Sequences (LABS) problem, which is a formidable computational challenge. In this problem we have to find binary sequences S_{L}^{*} of length L that have the highest value of the merit factor F, as shown in Eq. (1). These sequences are important in many areas, like communication engineering, statistical mechanics, chemistry, cryptography, and mathematics.

In our previous works we proposed two solvers, lssOrel and xLastovka. Both of them are stochastic solvers that use the mechanism for fast evaluation of neighbor solutions, and both are limited to skew-symmetric sequences. The main difference between them is the memory usage that guides the search process. lssOrel uses a self-avoiding walk and a small hash table so that the same pivot is not visited twice. xLastovka on the other hand stores a large number of promising sequences in a priority queue and uses them to manage the search process. Both solvers only explore the skew-symmetric search space. This means that the dimension of the search space is reduced by almost half (D=\frac{L+1}{2}), and so the solver can find (sub)-optimal sequences a lot faster. The skew-symmetric search space is only defined for odd instances, as shown in Eq. (2), and the optimal skew-symmetric sequences may not be optimal for the entire search space.

Other authors proposed a hybrid architecture that uses both CPU and GPGPU processing units for an agent-based memetic computational system. They used this system to solve the LABS problem on the entire search space with steepest descent and tabu search. The maximum speedup they got was 46 with tabu search for L=128. This result shows that GPGPU processing units are useful for solving the LABS problem. Because of this work, we proposed the sokol skew solver for skew-symmetric sequences. It is implemented for NVIDIA GPU devices using the CUDA (Compute Unified Device Architecture) toolkit. The sokol skew solver uses parallel self-avoiding walks and a recently published mechanism for efficient neighborhood evaluation. Both of them are computationally efficient and they also need only a small amount of memory. Together they are a suitable algorithm that prevents cycling and a mechanism that can use GPU devices to speed up the energy calculation. With them, sokol skew got a speedup of 387 compared to the sequential CPU solver, and so it found new best-known sequences.

In this paper we establish a predictive model of the stopping conditions for sokol skew, based on the instances from L=71 to L=119. With this model we determined the stopping conditions that the solver needs to reach the optimal skew-symmetric sequences with a probability of 99%. Using these stopping conditions, sokol skew found all the known and seven new best-known sequences for all odd instances from L=121 to L=223. We also used sokol skew for larger instances up to L=247, where it found all known and several new best-known sequences. We also calculated the probability that the sequences we got are optimal, according to the predictive model.

We also used all the best merit factor values to establish a model of their trend. The model shows that the merit factor values increase slightly as the sequence length increases, and that the trend is flatter for larger sequence sizes.

So the main contributions of this paper are:

- 1. A parallel search with self-avoiding walks for skew-symmetric sequences that uses GPGPU devices.

- 2. Skew-symmetric sequences for instances from L=121 to L=223 that are optimal with a probability of 99% according to the predictive model.

- 3. Seventeen new best-known sequences for L\leq 247.

- 4. The trend of merit factors based on the new best-known sequences.

The rest of the paper is organized like this. Section 2 describes related work. Section 3 describes the proposed sokol skew solver. Section 4 presents the experiments, the analysis of the proposed solver, and the results. Section 5 concludes the paper.
